title: No, the Phonics Decoding Advantage Does Not Persist For the Most Disadvantaged Readers
author: Freddie deBoer
summary: Freddie deBoer takes on a narrower claim than phonics triumphalism: that structured phonics at least lifts the most disadvantaged readers to a durable floor. He reads the Machin, McNally and Viarengo study of England's phased synthetic phonics rollout, where a 0.25 SD advantage at age five shrank to 0.08 SD at seven and zero by eleven. The persistence claim rests on a 0.06 SD subgroup result in one of two cohorts, which he calls practically trivial. He adds that the National Reading Panel and the Reading First evaluation found no significant comprehension benefit. His conclusion is that phonics is a sensible way to teach decoding but not an equity intervention, and that children who struggle at five mostly still struggle at fifteen.
points: The key study found a 0.25 SD phonics advantage at age five that faded to 0.08 SD at seven and to zero on average by eleven.
The claim of persistence for poor and ELL students comes from a 0.06 SD result in one of two cohorts, two significant results out of eight subgroup comparisons.
deBoer illustrates 0.06 SD with height (under a fifth of an inch) and IQ (less than one point) to show how little it means in practice.
He cites the National Reading Panel and Reading First as finding no significant comprehension effect beyond the earliest grades.
He concedes phonics is a sensible route to decoding, but argues it is being oversold as an equity intervention.
quotes: The people who advance this reading of the evidence make a specific empirical prediction, which is that the children at the bottom should gain more and keep those gains.
Five year olds in the early-adopting schools scored about .25SD higher in reading than their peers in schools that hadn’t yet switched to the structured phonics curriculum.
By age seven, the effect size difference had shrunk to about 0.08SD. By age eleven, the average effect was zero.
Two significant results out of eight subgroup comparisons seems like thin support for a sweep policy claims, but let’s take the .06SD advantage at face value.
Phonics teaches decoding, the ability to turn letters into sounds and sounds into words. Decoding is a necessary but insufficient part of the real goal, which is comprehension
Phonics is now being sold as an equity intervention, a way to lift the bottom of the distribution toward the middle.
Children who struggle to read at five mostly still struggle at fifteen, whatever method of teaching they receive.
